title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
description: As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides. Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than
body: As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides. Eating a kiwi with the skin on, external provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example. For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon. They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.For example:watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal breadbutternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakespineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the fleshbroccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the floretsFibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre."This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one; you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."The college has been experimenting in its canteen, external, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry. At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries, or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest. While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.Steaming, microwaving, or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.Dr Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try. Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial. Over the nine-week period, 'root-to-tip' dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university. Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds."Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people with IBS may find it harder to tolerate.And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation. Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

schema.headline: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say

title: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions
description: Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison
body: Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.Erin Patterson, 51, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said."We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.

schema.headline: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions

title: South Africa vs Australia: Careless dismissals give tourists route to series win
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The winner of the third Test will finish the series top of the International Cricket Council's Test rankingsB
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The winner of the third Test will finish the series top of the International Cricket Council's Test rankingsByMatthew HenryBBC Sport journalistThird Test, Cape Town (day three of five)South Africa 329 & 140-4: Ackerman 62; Starc 2-29Australia 429: Inglis 102; Harmer 4-104South Africa lead by 40 runsScorecardBatters carelessly gifting wickets to Australia... we have been here before.This time it was not England helping their opponents, although they will have taken note with a tour of South Africa to come this winter.South Africa's attempt to fight back in the decisive third Test against Australia was hurt by two poor strokes on day three.Having taken the last six Australian wickets for 99 runs in the morning despite Josh Inglis' second Test century, the Proteas began their second innings facing a deficit of exactly 100.They needed runs from their experienced opener and number three. Neither Aiden Markram nor David Bedingham could deliver.By the end, even captain Temba Bavuma had been tempted into a wild swipe to fall for 35. South Africa were 140-4, just 40 runs ahead, at the close.Australia are closing in.Weakness exposed by AustraliaIn isolation, Markram's drive off Mitchell Starc straight into the hands of mid-off for one appeared the most egregious.The ball was the fullest of the six balls Markram faced but not there for him to play his trademark shot. Fielder Travis Head did not have to move.Worse, though, was the dismissal of Bedingham, who showed he had not learned from the first innings.Then, the right-hander top-edged a pull to Josh Hazlewood off the bowling of Starc. This time he repeated the shot, with Hazlewood the wicket-taking bowler."That is just absolutely soft from David Bedingham," said former South Africa bowler Vernon Philander."He knew they were going to target him in that zone. For the second time in the Test, he has fallen to the same ploy."Image source, CricVizImage caption, The delivery which dismissed Markram was the fullest he had faced but still not full enough to be a driving length Given the prized position in South Africa's batting order on the back of strong domestic form for Durham in the County Championship and twin hundreds for Western Province in September, this score of 11 followed contributions of 49, 46 and 50 in his other four innings.He has got in but has not made a match-winning contribution.Batting in the key position of first drop, some would say that is more infuriating than not getting in at all.His dismissal, again like in the first innings, came shortly after being hit by a bouncer, with Starc clattering one into his chest on this occasion.When, after starting with two balls on a good length, Hazlewood went short again, Bedingham's eyes lit up.Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer and co should have been taking note. It was the fifth time he has been dismissed pulling in his 18 Tests. On average he gets out playing that shot once every 13 deliveries. "He never looks in the right position to play the pull or hook shot," former South Africa captain Graeme Smith said. "He is always off balance. He is never in a strong position."You think about best pullers in the game they have a strong base. He is pirouetting on one leg."[South Africa great] Hashim Amla just put the pull shot away for a phase."That is what a player like Bedingham needs to think about."Cummins tweak brings Bavuma wicketBavuma, in contrast, dug in for 115 balls in which he hit only one boundary.As he had in his 179 in the second-Test win in Gqeberha which set up this grand Cape Town finale, he showed his side the way in a partnership lasting 17.3 overs with Matthew Breetzke after opener Marques Ackerman had briskly made 65 before being bounced out by Starc.But with four minutes to go in the day, Australia captain Pat Cummins tweaked his field for spinner Nathan Lyon.Bavuma had pushed and driven outside off stump to that point but, with a silly point now in place, he was dragged from his crease and tried to force through mid-wicket.Australia's celebrations suggested they believe that was the crucial wicket.The vicious turn Lyon found means any chase over 200 would not be straightforward for Australia. South Africa's spinner Simon Harmer dismissed Inglis and Alex Carey (80) earlier in the day on his way to figures of 4-104.The Proteas have Breetzke and Ryan Rickelton at the crease - and Test triple-centurion Wiaan Mulder to come, before in-form all-rounder Marco Jansen and the tail.This still appears a tall order, however.As on day one and two, Australia have held firm and their opponents faltered. England know that feeling too.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Careless dismissals give tourists route to series win

title: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations
description: Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-pre
body: Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.They have made some bold promises. Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down. Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast."In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade."While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC."Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list."Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

schema.headline: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations

title: Cubans in Florida waver on Trump and Republicans over immigration
description: Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ism
body: Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ismael Labrador, in Miami is never empty. His appointment book is packed with relatives of detained immigrants trying to secure their release before they're deported back to their countries of origin.Although business is booming, Labrador wishes it wasn't."We have relatives living in fear right now, we've had relatives who have been deported back to Cuba, unfortunately," he explains.Cubans have traditionally enjoyed favoured immigration status in the United States under provisions enshrined in 1960s-era legislation called the Cuban Adjustment Act. But widespread arrests across Florida by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have left the Cuban American community more vulnerable in the US than they'd ever imagined, says Labrador."The way I put it is that if you don't have a Green Card in the United States, you may be a target."Countless mobile phone videos have recorded such arrests in places previously considered off-limits: parents detained outside schoolyards, at bus stops, youth sporting events and even inside courthouses at pre-arranged immigration hearings.Few have had the impact of the footage of 39-year-old Ecuadorean immigrant, Grace Calero, and her 19-year-old daughter, Giulianna Carriel, being arrested in a hospital ward.Two months ago, the pair were driving to work in Kissimmee, central Florida when they were hit by another car and taken to hospital in an ambulance. While they were being treated for their injuries, ICE agents burst in and arrested them. They were deported back to Ecuador within days.Labrador's cousin has also been caught up in the dragnet of ICE detentions. Despite his best efforts, the immigration lawyer was unable to prevent his own relative from being deported back to Cuba."It's hard when you're fighting against a lot of resources," he laments.The Trump administration has repeatedly said the president was elected on a promise to deliver mass deportations and is delivering on that. "He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," a White House spokeswoman told the BBC last week.ICE, meanwhile, has said it is targeting anyone who has broken American immigration law and is in the country illegally.GUIDE: What are the US midterms?IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians EXPLORE: Where the US midterms will be won and lostVERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under TrumpNEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inboxLabrador was among the 68% of Cuban Americans in Florida who voted for Donald Trump two years ago, a decision he roundly regrets today.Few could accuse Trump of hiding his plans on immigration. On the campaign trail in 2024, he touted his policy of mass deportations of undocumented migrants."On Day One, I will launch the largest deportation programme in American history", he said repeatedly at rallies, including in Florida.How Trump’s Cuba policy is shaping Miami’s midtermsLabrador – and many thousands of disillusioned Latino voters like him – thought the administration would only deport people with criminal records."I think we got blindsided by the administration," he argues."Personally, I voted for Trump because I wanted to get criminals out of the country," he says, alleging that "communists came in from Cuba under Biden.""We wanted to have a safe America. We never thought that he was going to go after everybody.""This isn't what I voted for," he insists.Labrador is far from the only Cuban American in Florida to experience buyer's remorse over President Trump.Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents Florida's 27th Congressional district, recently released a video filmed outside the White House in which she distanced herself from his deportation policy saying it had gone "too far"."The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said, addressing President Trump. Salazar is locked in a tight race against another Cuban American, the Democratic Party's candidate, Eliott Rodríguez. Her close association with Trump on immigration could potentially cost Salazar her congressional seat.Florida remains a Trump stronghold. At a recent gathering of Cuban American entrepreneurs in Miami, the atmosphere remained staunchly pro-Trump. "Miami loves Trump, Cuban Americans love Trump," says real estate businessman, Juan Omar Sixto, motioning at the other guests behind him."They agree with Trump that anyone who crossed the border illegally should be out," he says, despite acknowledging he illegally entered the US himself six decades earlier.A poll released on Thursday, external by Florida International University found that not all South Florida Cubans agree - 76% said they disapprove of the Trump administration's deportations of Cubans with no criminal record. But their support for the Republican Party remains steadfast, with 68% saying they plan to vote Republican in November. In other parts of the country, support amongst Latinos is declining.In the last election, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 56.1% to 43% - the biggest margin of victory for a candidate in the state since 1988 - in part because of the support of Latino communities. But a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll of 8,000 registered Latino voters showed nearly 60% favour seeing Congress come under Democratic Party control to just 35% wanting a Republican victory.The high cost of living is a big factor for people's discontent, as residents feel supermarket and petrol prices are impossibly high for working families.But for many Hispanics, it's also partly because of stories like Heydi Sanchez's.Sanchez left Cuba in 2019 as the island spiralled into economic collapse and illegally crossed the border from Mexico into the US. After nine months in a detention centre, she was released under an i-220B Order of Supervision which grants the right to remain in the US but carries the constant threat of deportation.Sanchez settled in Tampa where she worked with autistic children and the elderly. After a complex and expensive fertility struggle, she and her husband had a baby girl called Kailyn.Most i-220B holders try to normalise their immigration status via 'humanitarian parole' and must check in with ICE agents at regular scheduled appointments. Last year, President Trump revoked temporary humanitarian parole to about 300,000 Cubans. Sanchez knew something was wrong in her case when her regular ICE meeting was brought forward without warning.At the appointment, she was detained. Kailyn was taken from her arms and passed to her father, a US citizen. Within a day, Sanchez was on a deportation flight back to Havana in shackles with no recourse to appeal.I met her in Cuba where she now lives in a one-bed apartment in Mayabeque, a rural province outside Havana."It's like the sky fell in and crushed me", she says of being separated from her daughter."When we have video calls, she says: 'Mummy, come home.' And I say: 'darling, Mummy is away working.' What else can I tell her? How can I explain it?'", Sanchez asks, unable to hold back the tears.Despite expressions of support from several US politicians, including Maria Elvira Salazar, more than a year has passed since her deportation and Sanchez remains in limbo in Cuba.In a statement, ICE said that "in this case, the parent stated they wanted to be removed without the child and left the child in the care of a safe relative in the United States".While the Trump Administration has rolled back Cubans' special immigration privileges, it has sent thousands of people back to an island Washington itself describes as a "failed state". Cuba is in the grip of its worst ever energy crisis amid a months-long fuel blockade imposed by the US.Since overwhelmingly voting for Trump in 2024, Cubans in Florida now realise they are just as vulnerable to deportation as any other diaspora. His Republican colleagues may feel the brunt of their frustration at the ballot box.

schema.headline: Cubans in Florida waver on Trump and Republicans over immigration

title: The Traitors: Bombshell confession as faithfuls finally turn the screw
description: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.With the traitors still riding high following la
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.With the traitors still riding high following last Friday's episode, could they really just walk it to the final? It was time to find out.Having been bestowed with the almighty power of the double dagger - well, metaphorically speaking, at least - King Kenny held all the cards, choosing to use his special power of a double vote to send another faithful packing.As cliffhangers go, it wasn't hugely thrilling for viewers at home, given that the pair up for banishment - Sharon Rooney and Joanne McNally - were both faithfuls.Nevertheless, it left a big impact on the faithful crew as they realised they had let the traitors land yet another blow ahead of Friday's final."We've got to pull something out of the bag," said frustrated faithful Michael Sheen later. He wasn't wrong.Joanne got teary as she departed and joked "she was premenstrual," before revealing she was "a hardcore faithful". Maya described her as a "ball of fun", while Kenny put on his best acting skills in the aftermath by pretending to be struggling with having the deciding vote, even comforting poor Sharon. Give that man an Oscar.Meanwhile, James Blunt was on the hunt for whiskey like a teenager at the end of a house party: "Where do they keep the stiff stuff?" he asked himself, finding only a tray of empty glasses. Murder was soon on the minds of the traitors again as the dastardly trio of Kenny, Maya and James A trudged up to the turret."The life of a traitor... it's not for everyone," said Maya. And that probably includes James A, although to be fair, he has shown a bit more enthusiasm for some pantomime villainy in the last couple of episodes. More on him later."Let's have faith," said King Kenny without a hint of irony.As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.  "Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse."Vengeful daddy is in the house today."Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens."Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and FridayThe latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedBack at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table."I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped."I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards. And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DSI Sheen is on her case.

schema.headline: The Traitors: Bombshell confession as faithfuls finally turn the screw

title: Rocking repairs - why mended clothes are going mainstream
description: From workshops to the catwalk - why mended clothes are going mainstreamImage source, Alice Brown/MaybeArtUKImage caption, Alice Brown uses felt animal
body: From workshops to the catwalk - why mended clothes are going mainstreamImage source, Alice Brown/MaybeArtUKImage caption, Alice Brown uses felt animals to cover holes and stains on her clothesByLucy HookerBusiness reporterIf Alice Brown is browsing in second-hand shops and finds a jumper with a hole, that won't stop her buying it."I see it as challenge," says the 27-year-old forest ranger from Lincolnshire.She is a champion of the growing fashion for eye-catching repairs.Over the last year she has developed her own unique style, needle-felting cute animals and insects to cover moth holes, stains and other imperfections, winning her a huge following online."The natural place for decoration is in the centre at the front. If the hole is under the arm or on the shoulder, it forces you to think about the design," she says.Often dubbed "visible mending" the trend is spreading from hobby crafters and community workshops, even drawing in fast-fashion brands and reaching the designer catwalks this year. Image source, Jayne Eagle / The Stitching MagpieImage caption, Some mends are designed to be eye-catchingAt one Saturday morning workshop in Brighton, Jayne Eagle shows her students how to attach a patch of fabric behind a tear so the cat-face design peeps through.Then she instructs them in stitching techniques inspired by the traditional Japanese methods Boro and Sashiko. Instead of matching the thread colour to the garment, they make the mend highly decorative using geometric patterns in large white stitching.She also offers classes in darning using contrasting vibrant colours that celebrate, rather than disguise, the repair.Image caption, Jayne Eagle sees repair as an "act of rebellion" against fast fashionOne student, Nicola, has already used her newfound skills to stitch over sunscreen marks on a T-shirt "making a feature of it" and is now delighted that people "stop seeing the stains and just see the decoration". Another student, Lisa, says her mother's generation would never have wanted the mends to show. "Now part of it is being proud of what you've done," she says.Lisa bought a second-hand jacket online, but snipped the fabric with the scissors when she was opening the package. She managed to patch it in a way that "looks intentional"."I was actually pointing it out to people," she laughs.Image caption, Lisa says she's so proud of her mends she wants people to notice themIn the past mending was primarily about saving money, by wearing clothes for longer, rather than buying new. But visible mending is about celebrating that choice. The trend took off about six years ago, Jayne says, and has boomed since.An era of "throwaway" fast fashion from the 1980s onwards undermined the tradition of looking after and mending your clothes and people lost the skills, she says.The revival of interest feels to her like a backlash against overproduction in the fashion industry and the damage it causes: the pollution, carbon emissions, water use, and poor labour conditions.So perhaps it is surprising just how popular mended style is proving among retailers, with brands from Ralph Lauren to ultra-fast-fashion firm Shein currently selling stitched and patched garments, albeit in both of those cases brand new off the peg.Other High Street chains are adopting a more authentic approach, offering in-house repairs and workshops."We want to give customers practical ways to extend the life of the clothes they already love, rather than simply replacing them," says Uniqlo's head of sustainability, Maria Ledous.Image source, Oscar Elliot/UniqloImage caption, Uniqlo offers decorative mending using Sashiko techniques, in keeping with the brand's Japanese heritagePrimark, often seen as a fast-fashion retailer due to its lower prices, has also joined the trend."We don't think that affordability and durability should be opposites," says Vicki Swain, the brand's longevity lead.Outdoor brand Finisterre says around a fifth of the mends it provides for customers are designed to be eye-catching, while premium artisan clothing store Toast says around a third of customers go for that option.Part of the "magic" is that customers can bring in a garment and "choose what they'd like it to become next", says Toast chief executive Suzie de Rohan Willner.Image source, Sukhi Dhanda/ToastImage caption, Toast has a team of 14 in-house "repair artists" providing a range of creative mendsToast's repair services are free, but off-the-peg "renewed" pieces fetch higher prices than the originals to reflect their unique character.Levi's, which boasts probably the longest tradition of being fixed up by its fans using anything from rhinestones to fringed cuffs, is rolling out a workshop programme this year.The firm says its research shows younger customers in particular want to repair more but don't know how. For now, Levi's' workshops focus on traditional mending skills, such as sewing on a button and hemming, rather than visible mends, and at a recent launch event in London, that seemed to be what its Gen Z participants were looking for."I'm from East London. If you have holes in your clothes people are like 'Ha ha! You're poor!'," says 16-year-old school student Bianca.Image caption, At a workshop run by Levi's, Nicholas (r) says he prefers mending not to show, while Bianca (centre) says people still see it as a sign of povertyTheo, 19, says he'd rather learn how to mend without it showing."I would want [the jeans] to look how I originally bought them," he says. He has a side hustle selling clothes at car boot sales and thinks traditional repair skills would make it more lucrative.His friend Nicholas, also 19, says most people want to look "fresh"."No-one wants to look like they came out of a dumpster," he says. Still, Paul Dillinger, Levi's head of global design innovation, thinks more creative repairs will win them over as they pick up more skills."No-one has time for that perfect 'straight from the shop' thing. That's not cool. "People crave agency," he says. "Mending is a demonstration of humanity: it's not a mustard stain, it's a memory of a great day in the ballpark."

schema.headline: Rocking repairs - why mended clothes are going mainstream

title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Activists with a placard saying "Love your neighbour" urge opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot to try to
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Activists with a placard saying "Love your neighbour" urge opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government that includes Arab-led partiesByTom BennettReporting fromJerusalemThe main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey. Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference. Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless. The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.Image source, EPAImage caption, Arab-led parties including the Joint List headed by Yousef Jabareen (C) won a record 19 seats and could play a kingmaker roleIsraeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.Figure caption, Netanyahu shares AI image on day of Israeli electionArab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

schema.headline: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election

title: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
description: Rachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be
body: Rachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together. Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Mount Snowdon. But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister."And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother."I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler."

schema.headline: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart

title: Jack Grealish: What next for England winger after 'breach of club discipline'?
description: David Moyes says it was the club's decision to leave Jack Grealish out of Everton's Carabao Cup win over Newcastle United because of "a breach of club
body: David Moyes says it was the club's decision to leave Jack Grealish out of Everton's Carabao Cup win over Newcastle United because of "a breach of club discipline".Everton did not disclose any further details, but the decision is understood to have arisen from an unauthorised absence from training."You probably know I'm not going to give any details," said Moyes after Everton's 3-1 win at Hill Dickinson Stadium set up a quarter-final tie at League Two Fleetwood Town."It's a club decision, it's something I don't want to speak too much about."Moyes made it clear he supported the decision to leave out England winger Grealish, 31, who is on loan from Premier League rivals Manchester City.Grealish spent a large chunk of last season with the Toffees under a similar arrangement, scoring twice and providing six assists in 20 appearances, before sustaining a season-ending foot injury in January.He returned to City and came on as a substitute during their 3-0 Community Shield defeat by Arsenal at Wembley in August.The former Aston Villa player, who cost City £100m in 2021, also featured as a substitute during their 2-1 win over Bournemouth on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.He rejoined Everton before the transfer window closed and has featured five times for them this season in the Premier League.Grealish also played in Everton's EFL Cup third-round win over Wolves.Asked if Grealish would return for the Premier League game at Newcastle on Monday, Moyes added: "I wouldn't give any team news away."Grealish is in the final year of his reported £300,000-a-week contract at Manchester City.He was discarded by Pep Guardiola in the Spaniard's final season in charge, being allowed to join Everton on a season-long loan deal.There were moments where he looked to be getting back to his best while playing for the Toffees before his foot injury.Such was his form at the beginning of last season, he claimed the Premier League's player-of-the-month award for August and quickly became a fans' favourite."He is a player who has fallen in love with the right shade of blue, but ultimately he is a City player and we have to respect that," Everton chief executive Angus Kinnear told BBC Radio Merseyside in August."What I do know is that the supporters and the team embraced him and treated him as one of our own. That gave us a good platform to have a longer term conversation with him."The most important thing is that he is back fit after he had a serious injury, so I was delighted to see him get some minutes in the Community Shield."Grealish impressed to such an extent last season that Moyes openly spoke about how much the player was "loved" at the club.The mood, however, appears to have changed.At a time when the Everton boss is relying on all his senior players to step up after a disappointing summer transfer window left his squad thin, there are now questions about whether Grealish's breach of club discipline will be the beginning of the end of his career at Everton.Grealish missed last Saturday's 2-0 defeat at Arsenal with illness and, according to reports,, external missed training on Monday without permission.He returned to training at Everton's Finch Farm complex but is expected to be fined for his unauthorised absence.Grealish has 39 England caps and has scored four goals for his country. He has not played for the Three Lions since scoring in a 3-1 Nations League win against Finland in Helsinki in 2024.Everton, who have not won a major trophy since 1995, did not need him as they brushed past Newcastle to reach the last eight of the EFL Cup.While Moyes refused to go into details about the breach of discipline, he did praise the players on duty on Thursday for not allowing Grealish's absence to distract them in what was an important cup tie."The one thing about Everton is that it has got good values behind it," added Moyes. "All the players stand up to the values on pitch and off the pitch. "The players did a brilliant job tonight. "We are limited in some areas but we are doing our best to keep challenging."

schema.headline: Jack Grealish: What next for England winger after 'breach of club discipline'?

title: CCTV shows frying pan used to stop Huntingdon train attacker
description: Figure caption, Watch: Footage from inside the train was shown to the jury at Cambridge Crown Court on ThursdayByPhil Shepkaat Cambridge Crown CourtCC
body: Figure caption, Watch: Footage from inside the train was shown to the jury at Cambridge Crown Court on ThursdayByPhil Shepkaat Cambridge Crown CourtCCTV footage of a crew member using a frying pan to fend off a knifeman aboard a train has been shown in court.Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Samir Zitouni showed "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives and defend others", during the mass stabbing on the Doncaster to London King's Cross train.Jurors at Cambridge Crown Court saw footage of Zitouni using the pan against Anthony Williams, before the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies attempting to murder 10 people aboard the train, three people in Peterborough the day before and a boy at a London railway station.The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.Image source, British Transport PoliceImage caption, The jury has been shown this image of Anthony Williams on a trainOn the second day of the trial, Paxton told jurors the attack on Zitouni was "prolonged, persistent and brutal".Zitouni was said to have told the defendant: "We love you, we can help you."Other CCTV footage played in court showed people fleeing the train. Zitouni, in what Paxton called a "blood-soaked shirt", appeared "to be one of the last off the train", and Paxton said he fell "between, essentially, the gap between the train and the platform".Figure caption, Footage of Williams' arrest and passengers fleeing was shown to the juryThe court heard both of Zitouni's lungs had been punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.Paxton earlier said one of the passengers, Raza Aslam, had grabbed a frying pan, but was stabbed in the hand by Williams.He said Zitouni started throwing things at the defendant and "saved" Aslam's life.Jurors also heard that Aslam told police Williams "had the greatest delight on his face".Aslam said: "I saw his eyes expand with pleasure. I saw the contempt on his face, like a person who's high."He was just loving every single moment. He loved seeing us in desperation."Image source, British Transport PoliceImage caption, The jury has been shown this image of Anthony Williams at Peterborough Railway Station, where he boarded the trainPaxton also told the jury how there was hand-to-hand fighting on the train.He said Sachin Balakrishnan was stabbed in the forearm and chest, which punctured a lung and was "just centimetres from his heart".The jury heard a call Stephen Crean made to 999 from a locked toilet on the train, telling the operator he had been stabbed "all over" and left "covered in blood".Figure caption, Huntingdon train victim Stephen Crean called 999 from a locked toiletCommenting on CCTV footage, Paxton said: "You can see the panic, you can see the fear in the faces of those fleeing."In this storm of violence, and even when gripped by fear, many there on that train helped others and, as we will see, some stood tall, quite literally, against the defendant's violent onslaught."Jurors also heard how Scott Green had been travelling on the train with his dog, Poppy.Paxton said: "He thought he was going to lose his life on the train when the defendant tried to stab him for the third time."It seems, members of the jury, that Poppy the dog, for Mr Green at least, saved the day and sent the defendant running off. "You will hear that in an unrelated incident the defendant had previously been bitten by a dog."Huntingdon Train Attack: Day OneFollowing the trial of Anthony Williams from Peterborough who is accused of carrying out multiple stabbing attacks on a train in Cambridgeshire in 2025, and separate attacks.During Thursday's evidence, the court was also told of an attack on 73-year-old David Presland, who had been stabbed in the back while on his hands and knees.Presland said he had been "helped by someone he knew as Kevin" - believed to be Kevin Deely, another of those Williams is accused of attempting to murder.Paxton told the court the events were "all over in about five minutes", adding: "In that time, 10 men are stabbed by one man, this defendant, Mr Williams."Williams is accused of attempting to murder Aslam, Balakrishnan, Crean, Deely, Green, Presland and Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on the Saturday evening, along with Scott Bletcher, Jonathan Gjoshe and Michael Paffett.He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.The trial continues.Additional reporting by Press Association.Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: CCTV shows frying pan used to stop Huntingdon train attacker

title: Tennis: Alexander Zverev to replace Jannik Sinner as ATP world number one after beating Tallon Girekspoor in Vienna
description: Zverev seals world number one spot after winImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Alexander Zverev is the 30th man to become the ATP world number o
body: Zverev seals world number one spot after winImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Alexander Zverev is the 30th man to become the ATP world number oneByBBC Sport tennis news reporterAlexander Zverev will replace Jannik Sinner as the men’s world number one at his earliest opportunity after reaching the quarter-finals in Vienna. He was already guaranteed to finish 2026 as the ATP’s leading player, but made sure he will rise to the summit on Monday with a 6-4 7-5 win over Tallon Griekspoor at the Erste Bank Open. Zverev, 29, is the second German to reach the pinnacle of the men's tour after Boris Becker in 1991.The achievement is a testament to his body of work this year, having won two Grand Slam titles and 64 of his 80 matches. "It's been a wait but sometimes you have to wait for the best things in life," said Zverev, who is the second oldest man to top the rankings for the first time."I'm super happy, super thrilled - I have no words for this year."At the start of the year it seemed unthinkable that anybody other than Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz would become world number one.But the dominant duo have missed large chunks of this season through injury, opening the door for Zverev - who won the French Open and US Open titles with at least one of the pair absent - to take over.Going into 2026, Alcaraz led the rankings with 12,050 points, closely followed by Sinner on 11,500.The pair's duopoly - splitting all of the eight Grand Slam titles in 2024 and 2025 between them - was illustrated by the huge gap to the rest of the field.Third-ranked Zverev had 5,110 points - closer numerically to the 2,221st player in the world than the top two.Both his major triumphs came without having to face Sinner or Alcaraz, and he did not face a top-10 player until beating Ben Shelton in the New York final.As the season entered its final stretch, Zverev achieved what many thought was impossible by securing the year-end number one ranking when Alcaraz lost in Shanghai on 12 October.Zverev knew he still could not overtake Sinner until 2 November at the earliest, but beat Griekspoor to become the first man other than Sinner and Alcaraz to top the rankings since Novak Djokovic in June 2024.Zverev conceded he would "maybe not" be the world's best player if both his rivals were "healthy and at the top of their game".But he has efficiently beaten what has been in front of him, recording the greatest season of a career which had threatened to fall short of the lofty expectations placed on him since emerging as a teenage prodigy.Fery continues to prove himself - and faces Zverev nextImage source, ReutersImage caption, Arthur Fery avenged a three-set defeat by Lorenzo Musetti in the US Open first round in AugustZverev goes on to face British number one Arthur Fery in the quarter-finals - a repeat of their Wimbledon semi-final.Fery, 24, made an unexpected run to the SW19 last four in July, but continued to prove he belongs among the world's best with a 6-4 5-7 6-4 win over Italy's Lorenzo Musetti in Vienna.Trailing 4-2 in the decider, Fery showed his mental fortitude by breaking straight back and then overcoming what seemed to be cramp to serve out an impressive victory.It is easy to forget Fery is still inexperienced at the elite level following his Wimbledon heroics.Beating former world number five Musetti - now ranked 26th after injury - represents his biggest win by ranking on the regular ATP Tour and provides another opportunity to test himself against the very best.However, Cameron Norrie fell short of his best victory of the season when world number five Daniil Medvedev saved match point to win their last-16 match.A frustrating year has seen Norrie drop to 41st in the world rankings and exit each of the past three Grand Slam tournaments in the first round.But the 31-year-old showed his key attributes - tenacity, athleticism and controlled aggression - to threaten a huge upset against Medvedev.Third seed Medvedev, fresh from winning the Almaty title last week, was left angrily punching the surface when he fell a break down in the deciding set.Norrie served for the match at 5-3 40-30, but Medvedev picked off his opponent's serve-volley attempt and fought back to win 4-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1).Second seed Alcaraz also progressed with a 6-1 7-6 (13-11) win over Georgia's Nikoloz Basilashvili.Meanwhile, Novak Djokovic's hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals were harmed by a second-round defeat at the Swiss Indoors event in Basel.The 24-time major champion, 39, lost 7-6 (7-4) 5-7 6-7 (5-7) to Germany's Jan-Lennard Struff, who produced some inspired tennis to beat the Serb for the first time in nine attempts.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An annoyed Medvedev hitting the court was seemingly a show of disdain for the speed of the surface

schema.headline: Tennis: Alexander Zverev to replace Jannik Sinner as ATP world number one after beating Tallon Girekspoor in Vienna

title: Hundreds of GP surgeries lose online services after Silicon Practice collapse
description: Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.Silicon Pract
body: Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected."If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them."When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams."It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.

schema.headline: Hundreds of GP surgeries lose online services after Silicon Practice collapse

title: Value of Google parent Alphabet plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
description: At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hi
body: At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.By the end of Thursday,  the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter. The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools."One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added."We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI."Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

schema.headline: Value of Google parent Alphabet plunges by $500bn as AI fears rattle Wall Street
